The 2027 Hyundai Ioniq 6 N Costs Nearly BMW M2 Coupe Money in Canada
7 photos
Photo: Hyundai
The Ioniq 6 N electric performance sedan is a rather expensive car, as expected from the outset. Destination and delivery pushes the newcomer into BMW M2 Coupe territory, and worse still for the South Korean automaker, the quicker and faster Tesla Model 3 Performance will set you back CAD 74,990 as of this writing.
Whichever way you look at it, that's considerable money for an electric performance model with an undesirable badge. On the other hand, the South Korean colossus has designed something considerably more ambitious than an Ioniq 6 with nicer wheels and a sporty-looking steering wheel.
The first N-badged Ioniq 6 uses two electric drive units and an 84- kWh battery pack, with Hyundai Canada promising 601 horsepower by default or 641 when N Grin Boost kicks in. Peak torque is estimated at 568 pound-feet (770 Newton-meters), and N Launch Control helps the zero-emission model reach 100 kilometers per hour (62 miles per hour) in a claimed 3.2 clicks.
Pretty impressive on paper, but N Grin Boost only enables maximum output for up to 10 seconds at a time. Beyond the powertrain side of the deal, Hyundai made some interesting chassis updates to cope with the additional oomph, starting with electronically controlled suspension that uses stroke sensors to adjust damping according to the selected drive mode and road conditions.
An electronic limited-slip diff is on the menu as well. What Hyundai calls N Torque Distribution allows the driver to adjust the front-rear torque bias, and the company has further revised the suspension geometry for this application. From a structural standpoint, more structural adhesives and additional weld points help the N stand out from lesser versions of the Ioniq 6.
Photo: Hyundai Almost 20 percent better in terms of torsional stiffness compared to standard 6s, the N rolls on Pirelli P Zero rubber that comes with 20-inch forged aluminum wheels. The 275/35 tires and lightweight wheels frame performance brakes, with Hyundai listing four-piston calipers up front.
A rear wing also differentiates it from lesser 6s. All in all, Hyundai has clearly spent a lot of time and money addressing on-road and on-track capability. Its high-voltage battery features dedicated temperature management functions, with N Battery Preconditioning offering different settings for three driving scenarios: Drag, Sprint, and Endurance. As implied, Drag is tailored for short bursts of maximum launch and acceleration performance.
With the Ioniq 6 N, the South Korean manufacturer is also selling an experience. N e-Shift is a system that simulates the behavior of a transmission, manipulating torque in the process. N Active Sound+, meanwhile, is the function that generates driving sounds to bring the Ioniq 6 N closer to internal combustion models like Hyundai's very own Elantra N performance sedan.
While certain enthusiasts will enjoy this tech-heavy theater, others might question the need to imitate a gas-powered performance car in the first place. I certainly understand what Hyundai is trying to achieve here, but fake shifts and powertrain sounds will get old rather quickly from the driver's perspective.
On a different note, Hyundai Canada confirmed a NACS port for a direct connection between it and Tesla Superchargers. No need for adapters here! Unfortunately, the Canadian-market announcement does not provide specific driving range and energy consumption figures. In any case, the first units will hit dealer lots in early 2027, and Hyundai Canada underlines that limited quantities are expected.
